jokes.text: Oh, my God. It's the people coming to stop the show. / Oh, now what do we do? / We have to stop the people. Their freedom of speech depends on it. / Frankie, Chang, bar the doors.
jokes.setup: The group committed to protecting free speech now faces a crowd of people exercising their free speech to stop the show.
jokes.punchline: 'We have to stop the people. Their freedom of speech depends on it.' — the full satirical reversal lands. Protecting free speech now means physically restraining people from speaking.
jokes.explanation: The satirical reversal completes here with Jeff's earnest 'we have to stop the people' — perfectly capturing how free speech absolutism can flip into its opposite when tested. Good structural comedy as well as sharp writing.

jokes.text: Hey, y'all. Look, I see there's a lot of Jews in the crowd. I mean, you know, there isn't, but usually when I do my act there's more, but you know, I have a whole Jew thing. / Do it. / Okay, okay. Who's this guy? / Stop performing. / Do not stop performing.
jokes.setup: Gupta finally performs. The threatened crowd tries to shut him down from outside.
jokes.punchline: His opening bit is immediately disrupted — both by the hostile crowd and by the absurdity of him describing his own unperformed material ('I have a whole Jew thing'). Jeff and the interrupter give him contradictory commands simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: The chaos of the performance — interrupters, defenders, the comedian narrating his own routine rather than performing it — is good structural comedy. The 'I have a whole Jew thing' meta-announcement is funny precisely because it describes the joke rather than making it.

jokes.text: It's hard to be fat when you're black or Jewish because when you're black your community steals all your food, so you can't eat as much, and when you're Jewish, nobody ever buys anything, so you can't eat as much. / You're damned if you do. You're damned if you don't. / Ugh. Oh, dear God.
jokes.setup: Gupta finally performs his act as the crowd tries to storm the room.
jokes.punchline: His jokes are genuinely bad — lazy stereotype-stacking delivered with impeccable earnestness, landing to universal groans — the comedy being the gap between his confidence and the content.
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Gupta's comedy is bad — deliberately so. The structure ('you're damned if you do, you're damned if you don't' as the punchline to bad stereotypes) is internally consistent with how a mediocre provocateur would operate. The comedy comes from the audience's cringe, not from the material itself. The show is using bad comedy purposefully, which requires craft — but it's a metatextual joke, not a first-order one.

jokes.text: Have you found anyone else you could love, like another fat person, or are you one of those fat people who will always be alone?
jokes.setup: Gupta continues performing as chaos erupts around him.
jokes.punchline: He singles out the one-person audience with an audience-interaction bit that is both his worst and most direct material — asking a fat man if he'll die alone.
jokes.explanation: Intentionally bad — the joke's value is in illustrating Gupta's cruelty and incompetence, not in the content itself. The fact that it's aimed at the only audience member makes it structurally worse-as-comedy, which is functionally the right choice for the show's purposes.

jokes.text: Hey, Leonard! / You enjoy my girlfriend in 2009? / As much as she enjoyed your plagiarized poetry. / I will kill you!
jokes.setup: The leaked emails have caused everyone to attack everyone else.
jokes.punchline: Jeff attacks Leonard over a 2009 girlfriend; Leonard fires back about plagiarized poetry; Jeff threatens murder — escalating from personal grievance to genuine threat.
jokes.explanation: Good Leonard moment — his escalation from romantic revelation to devastating counter-attack ('plagiarized poetry') is sharp. 'I will kill you!' from Jeff is a proper escalation. The specificity of a 2009 girlfriend and plagiarized poetry implies a whole backstory.

jokes.text: Don't act like you care about me! I've seen all your cartoons about me! / I am this school's worst nightmare! I am a Garrett with no soul left to steal!
jokes.setup: Everyone's private grievances are erupting simultaneously during the show.
jokes.punchline: Garrett's declaration — 'I am a Garrett with no soul left to steal' — is a surprisingly self-aware villain-speech delivered by the school's most pathetic recurring character.
jokes.explanation: 'I am a Garrett with no soul left to steal' is instantly legendary for Community fans. The joke operates on pure character comedy — Garrett as a proper noun used in a villain speech, with the implication that having a Garrett-soul is inherently less concerning than losing it. It's both self-deprecating and unexpectedly badass. Very high quotability and rewatch value.

jokes.text: Man, it's like Road Warrior out there, but if petrol were privacy and bad teeth were dirty secrets.
jokes.setup: Total chaos has broken out in the school as leaked emails cause everyone to fight.
jokes.punchline: Abed provides film-critic framing for the chaos, mapping the Road Warrior dystopia onto the email privacy scandal with perfect internal logic.
jokes.explanation: Classic Abed — applies a genre framework to real life with his characteristic precision. 'If petrol were privacy and bad teeth were dirty secrets' is a great parallel construction. The specific choice of Road Warrior (not just 'Mad Max') signals Abed's film-nerd specificity. High character integration and quotability.

jokes.text: Good news. Neil's talking to us again. He says he respects our moral position but not our execution. Also he says he's never talking to us again.
jokes.setup: The group has failed to protect the audience member Neil from public humiliation.
jokes.punchline: Neil's message is delivered as 'good news' — he's talking to them again — immediately contradicted by the final sentence: 'he's never talking to us again.'
jokes.explanation: Classic self-canceling message structure. 'Good news: he's talking to us' / 'He's never talking to us again' is a tight and well-timed reversal. The addition of 'he respects our moral position but not our execution' adds useful texture.

jokes.text: If you follow a theme of revealed secrets, the email hack is the third installment of a trilogy that began with Annie losing a pen in what I've come to call the golden age.
jokes.setup: The group is processing the disaster.
jokes.punchline: Abed reframes the entire history of the show as a trilogy structure, with 'Annie losing a pen' as the genesis event — the pilot episode reduced to its most trivial element.
jokes.explanation: Excellent meta-reference for Community fans. Calling the pilot's inciting incident ('Annie losing a pen') the beginning of 'the golden age' is a wink to devoted viewers. Abed framing the show's events as film-trilogy installments is perfectly in character. High meta-value and quotability.

jokes.text: I'm guessing the second chapter would be when your best friend vanished on a mysterious boat trip after the older one masturbated himself to death?
jokes.setup: Abed proposes the email hack is part of a trilogy of revealed secrets in their history.
jokes.punchline: Jeff references the actual real-life departures from the show — a character who 'vanished on a mysterious boat trip' (Troy on a sailing trip) and 'the older one masturbated himself to death' (the Chevy Chase firing/character death) — reframing cast shake-ups as in-universe events.
jokes.explanation: Meta-joke requiring show knowledge. The euphemisms for how Troy and Pierce left the show are both funny in themselves ('vanished on a mysterious boat trip,' 'masturbated himself to death') and function as meta-commentary on the real departures. 'The older one masturbated himself to death' is an extraordinary sentence. Very high rewatch bonus for viewers who catch the reference.

jokes.text: If that's one you guys bounced back from, we might be okay.
jokes.setup: Jeff's dark recap of the show's history (Troy leaving, Pierce dying).
jokes.punchline: Gupta, an outsider, processes this as evidence of resilience rather than the dark tragedy it is.
jokes.explanation: Good button to the meta-sequence. Gupta as outside observer offering naive encouragement is a solid comedic role.

jokes.text: What's the lesson here? I always want to make sure I know what the lesson is. I'm a completist.
jokes.setup: The group is processing the episode's events.
jokes.punchline: Gupta expresses a desire for moral closure — 'I always want to make sure I know what the lesson is. I'm a completist.' — which mirrors the audience's own viewing experience, delivered by a terrible comedian as though he's taking notes.
jokes.explanation: Meta-joke about TV episode structure — the character asking for the lesson mirrors the audience. 'I'm a completist' is a funny addition that characterizes Gupta as someone who approaches his own bad comedy with academic rigor.

jokes.text: The rest of the school's in shambles, so maybe we're more evolved and forgiving than them? / We already know that, stupid.
jokes.setup: Someone offers a lesson from the episode.
jokes.punchline: Jeff dismisses the self-congratulatory lesson — not because it's wrong, but because they already knew it. The self-awareness of being self-aware.
jokes.explanation: 'We already know that, stupid' is a good Jeff line — refusing the sentimental lesson not by disagreeing but by claiming prior knowledge. It's the show commenting on its own meta-awareness without being too pleased with itself.

jokes.text: I feel more desensitized to jokes about Jews and blacks. Is that good? / Say what?
jokes.setup: The group is trying to find the lesson of the episode.
jokes.punchline: Someone offers their personal takeaway — moral desensitization to racist jokes — as though it might be a valid lesson. The 'Say what?' response perfectly captures the room's (and audience's) reaction.
jokes.explanation: Good dark beat — 'Is that good?' delivered with genuine uncertainty is funny. The 'Say what?' reaction is exactly right. The show is willing to acknowledge that its own episode might have produced a bad lesson.

jokes.text: We know the pieces are privacy, freedom of speech, terrorism, and government, so the lesson is probably an ironic pairing like one man's privacy is another man's freedom. / Government is terrorism? / The only free speech is private speech. / A free government terrorizes privacy. / That's all four, bitches. / Terror is terrorized by... Terry the Terrorist? / Tarry not, for terrorism terrifies. / Govern the government. Freedom of speech.
jokes.setup: The group tries to workshop the episode's thematic lesson.
jokes.punchline: What begins as genuine thematic analysis quickly dissolves into word-salad portmanteaus: 'Terry the Terrorist,' 'Tarry not for terrorism terrifies,' 'Govern the government.' The escalation into meaninglessness is itself the lesson about trying to extract lessons.
jokes.explanation: One of Community's most self-aware moments — the group literally workshopping the episode's theme and arriving at nonsense is a perfect meta-commentary on TV moral closure. 'That's all four, bitches' as a moment of triumph before it falls apart is great escalation. 'Terry the Terrorist' landing as the peak of dissolution is funny. High rewatch value for how precisely it skewers TV convention.

jokes.text: We caught the hacker. This is Ryan aka 'String Cheese Hustler' aka 'Fart Mitzvah,' 'SkullandBoners88,' 'Frozen Sucked,' 'Captain Titty.' You don't need to know all his names.
jokes.setup: The case is resolved; Warburton brings in the hacker.
jokes.punchline: The hacker's aliases are an escalating list of absurd usernames: 'String Cheese Hustler,' 'Fart Mitzvah,' 'SkullandBoners88,' 'Frozen Sucked,' 'Captain Titty' — each one funnier than the last.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most purely funny joke lists. Each username is carefully chosen: 'String Cheese Hustler' (earnest food hustle), 'Fart Mitzvah' (juvenile-sacred mashup), 'SkullandBoners88' (generic edgelord), 'Frozen Sucked' (cultural critic), 'Captain Titty' (inexplicable naval rank). The escalation and variety are excellent, and 'You don't need to know all his names' as the button is perfect. High quotability.

jokes.text: I'm sorry. For what? / For guessing your school master password was 'change me.'
jokes.setup: The hacker is asked to apologize.
jokes.punchline: His apology is specifically for 'guessing' the password was 'change me' — the most basic default password, implying Greendale's security was defeated by a first-guess default.
jokes.explanation: 'Change me' as the master password is a perfect institutional-incompetence gag. The hacker apologizing not for hacking but for the ease of it is a good structural inversion. It retroactively makes the whole episode's stakes funnier.

jokes.text: Oops.
jokes.setup: It's revealed the school's master password was 'change me' — a default that Pelton presumably set.
jokes.punchline: Pelton's one-word acknowledgment of institutional negligence.
jokes.explanation: Perfect character beat — Pelton's 'Oops' acknowledges the entire episode's premise (he set 'change me' as the password at the start) with one word. Maximum economy, completely in character.

jokes.text: How do you sleep at night, Warburton? / You were one of us. You were free. / No one's free when they're one of anything, and to answer your question, I sleep alone with one eye open. That's why I'm not the one in cuffs. / Let's go, Fart Mitzvah.
jokes.setup: The hacker asks Warburton how he sleeps.
jokes.punchline: Warburton delivers a strangely philosophical hardboiled-cop speech — 'I sleep alone with one eye open' — then punctures it immediately by calling the hacker 'Fart Mitzvah.'
jokes.explanation: 'Let's go, Fart Mitzvah' is the perfect undercutting of the hardboiled speech. Warburton's commitment to using the alias after the philosophical speech is excellent. 'No one's free when they're one of anything' is also a good line — genuinely interesting delivered by a man who is about to say 'Fart Mitzvah.'

jokes.text: Let's go, Fart Mitzvah.
jokes.setup: Warburton has just delivered a philosophical speech about freedom.
jokes.punchline: He immediately deflates his own gravitas by using 'Fart Mitzvah' as the hacker's address — cutting from philosophical to toilet humor.
jokes.explanation: Three words, perfect economy. The callback to 'Fart Mitzvah' from the alias list is timed impeccably — it comes immediately after Warburton's most philosophical line, making the bathos complete. 'Let's go, Fart Mitzvah.' is one of the episode's most quotable lines. The deflation of his own gravitas is exactly the right move.

jokes.text: I'm sorry if I used photography to digitally approximate some of your naked bodies. / It's all right. / It is? No!
jokes.setup: In the aftermath, Elroy apologizes for the 3D modeling.
jokes.punchline: Someone says 'It's all right,' and Annie immediately overrides it — 'It is? No!' — refusing to let the apology be accepted.
jokes.explanation: Good callback coda. Annie's 'It is? No!' is the right character response — she is not letting this slide just because someone else accepted the apology. Good economy.

jokes.text: Same as yesterday. Big cloud of data raining over a pasture. All 8 billion sheep keep grazing. / Is that good? / Sure.
jokes.setup: Someone asks Warburton what's happening with the leaked data aftermath.
jokes.punchline: His pastoral metaphor — 'big cloud of data raining over a pasture, all 8 billion sheep keep grazing' — frames humanity's indifference to privacy as a sheep-grazing tableau, with 'Is that good? Sure.' as the deadpan resignation.
jokes.explanation: 'Big cloud of data raining over a pasture / all 8 billion sheep keep grazing' is a genuinely good metaphor delivered as a cop's status report. The flatness of 'Is that good? Sure.' is perfect Warburton — his cynicism expressed through pastoral imagery is a distinctive character voice.

jokes.text: That thing you said back there about not being a part of anything. Is that really how you feel? / It's not a question of how I feel. I feel like flying, I don't jump off buildings.
jokes.setup: Jeff probes Warburton's nihilism.
jokes.punchline: Warburton's response — 'I feel like flying, I don't jump off buildings' — is a good philosophical non-answer that uses a physical analogy to dismiss the question while actually answering it.
jokes.explanation: Good hardboiled-cop aphorism. 'I feel like flying, I don't jump off buildings' is quotable and captures Warburton's character — a pragmatic man who has decided feelings are irrelevant to decisions. Good economy.

jokes.text: Common courtesy's just gibberish. Hocus pocus. A spell we cast when hoping to cheat reality.
jokes.setup: Jeff invokes common courtesy as a bridge between people.
jokes.punchline: Warburton dismisses 'common courtesy' as hocus pocus — magical thinking deployed to avoid facing reality — delivered with flat philosophical conviction.
jokes.explanation: 'Hocus pocus. A spell we cast when hoping to cheat reality.' is a nicely constructed nihilist aphorism. Warburton's philosophical hardboiled voice is a consistent character note that makes these late-episode moments funny in a quieter register.

jokes.text: You're a cynical son of a bitch. I'll give you that. / You know, my wife, she makes these dreamcatchers... / Shh. Shut the hell up.
jokes.setup: Jeff acknowledges Warburton's nihilism; Warburton begins a touching story about his wife.
jokes.punchline: Warburton stops himself with 'Shh. Shut the hell up' — the character refuses his own moment of warmth, consistent with his established philosophy.
jokes.explanation: Perfect character closing moment. Warburton begins to open up with the dreamcatcher story — a moment of genuine warmth — then immediately shuts himself down, 'Shh. Shut the hell up.' It's both funny and poignant. The character's internal consistency is preserved: he literally won't let himself be one of anything, including one of the people who has feelings about dreamcatchers.

jokes.text: How fast can you get us to the mainframe hardline? / Yankee doodle dandy.
jokes.setup: Warburton needs to solve something urgent.
jokes.punchline: Elroy's response — 'Yankee doodle dandy' — is a completely inexplicable phrase as a readiness answer, delivered with apparent confidence.
jokes.explanation: Perfect closing callback to the episode's opening mainframe joke. The 'hardline' is referenced again, but Elroy's response — 'Yankee doodle dandy' — is an absurdist American affirmation that makes no literal sense but works as a 'ready to go' signal. The callback gives the episode structural closure. 'Yankee doodle dandy' as a battle cry is inexplicably funny.

jokes.text: You're a cynical son of a bitch. I'll give you that. / You know, my wife, she makes these dreamcatchers... / Shh. Shut the hell up.
jokes.setup: Jeff acknowledges Warburton's cynicism, which Warburton accepts.
jokes.punchline: Warburton begins what appears to be a humanizing anecdote about his wife's dreamcatchers — only to be immediately shut down by Jeff ('Shh. Shut the hell up.') before the warmth can land.
jokes.explanation: Perfect subversion of the 'hard-boiled cop reveals he has a soft side' trope. The setup — Warburton begins the dreamcatcher anecdote — primes for a moment of unexpected warmth, and Jeff immediately kills it. 'Shh. Shut the hell up.' is a perfect non-sentimental closer. The joke is about refusing the sentimental beat as a genre move, which is very Community.
